title: Container Security Basics
intro: A container is not a security boundary by default — it runs as root unless told otherwise, and ships whatever vulnerable packages its base image contains. These are the habits that close the most common gaps.

steps.prompt: Check which user the 'web' container's main process is actually running as.
steps.explanation: Root inside the container. If an attacker exploits the app, they're root in the container — and one kernel or misconfiguration bug away from root on the host.
steps.why: Most official base images default to root because it's convenient, not because it's needed — checking this directly beats assuming the Dockerfile author added a USER instruction.

steps.prompt: Run the container as an unprivileged user (UID 1000) instead, without rebuilding the image.
steps.explanation: --user overrides the image's default user at runtime.
steps.why: The permanent fix is a 'USER appuser' line in the Dockerfile so the image is safe by default — --user is the quick runtime override when you can't rebuild yet, and a good way to test whether the app actually needs root at all (usually it doesn't).

steps.prompt: Scan the 'myapp:v2' image for known vulnerabilities in its packages.
steps.fake_output:
myapp:v2
  CRITICAL: 2  HIGH: 7  MEDIUM: 19
  openssl 3.0.2  CVE-2024-XXXX  CRITICAL  fixed in 3.0.13
  (most findings come from the base image node:20)
steps.explanation: Most vulnerabilities come from the base image, not your own code — which is why upgrading the FROM line often fixes the majority at once.
steps.why: docker scout is built into recent Docker; trivy is the common open-source alternative used in CI pipelines. Either is far better than nothing — the real habit is running a scan in CI on every build, so a new CRITICAL fails the pipeline instead of reaching production.

steps.prompt: Run the container with a read-only root filesystem, allowing writes only to /tmp.
steps.explanation: An attacker who gets code execution can't drop files or modify binaries inside the container — the filesystem simply refuses writes outside /tmp.
steps.why: This is the Docker equivalent of Kubernetes' readOnlyRootFilesystem security context (tutorial-027). It breaks apps that write to unexpected paths, which is useful information in itself: you find out exactly where the app writes, and can mount just those paths as writable.

steps.prompt: Check whether any container is running in privileged mode — a major red flag.
steps.explanation: Privileged containers get essentially full access to the host's devices and kernel capabilities — almost never needed for application workloads.
steps.why: --privileged is often added as a copy-pasted 'fix' for a permissions error without understanding what it grants. Auditing for it is one of the fastest high-value security checks on any Docker host.
